vignette: Two years ago, Rania, a fifty-nine-year-old police officer of Middle Eastern descent, was driving home from a midnight shift when a silver sedan abruptly cut across her lane and slammed into her passenger door. The impact sent a jolt through her frame, but the violence that followed remained the most vivid part of the memory. The driver climbed out without checking his vehicle, stormed to her window, and began shouting. He gripped the roof and punched it hard, the metallic clang echoing in her ears. Rania watched him, her hands white-knuckled on the wheel, her heart hammering against her ribs. The responding officers were absorbed in their own paperwork, and the man walked away without a citation. Rania sat in the idling patrol car for nearly an hour, listening to the rhythm of her own pulse, certain that the unfairness of his departure left a quiet mark she carried forward. The memories that followed were sharp and detailed. When Rania closed her eyes, she could still hear the specific crack of the man’s knuckles against steel and the low whine of her dashboard light. Remembering the assault brought back the exact terror she had felt in that moment, as though the past and present occupied the same space. She found herself constantly checking her own thoughts, scanning them for any sign that she was unraveling. She kept a quiet ledger, noting every flutter in her chest and every spike of adrenaline, aware that her body was reacting as if the danger were still present, even while she stood safely in her kitchen. Over the next several months, her habits hardened. She declined invitations, gradually cutting off contact with friends and family until her phone mostly gathered digital dust. When she stepped outside, she scanned every passerby with a quiet alertness, reading strangers for potential threat. A man adjusting his coat, a woman speaking too loudly, a child running into the street—each moment sat alongside her steady breathing. Her avoidance extended to the driver’s seat as well. While she still took the patrol car to work, having a passenger in the front seat introduced a new tension. She would grip the steering wheel, her heart racing whenever the person beside her reached for the gear shift, her mind fixed on the possibility of sudden violence. The demands of her job made these shifts visible. At the precinct, Rania’s uniform felt like a familiar weight. She noticed how colleagues sometimes left conversations mid-sentence to check their phones, a gesture that aligned with her conviction that she could not rely on others when it mattered. Her husband’s quiet presence at the dinner table sat comfortably beside her own watchfulness, neither pulling her forward nor holding her back. She found herself retreating to the archives or taking extra patrol hours to maintain her distance, and the isolation and the alertness moved through her days like twin currents, simply occupying the same space. It was the quiet erosion of her daily rhythm that finally brought Rania to the clinic. She no longer wanted to sit in the waiting room bracing for another false alarm, nor did she wish to spend another year monitoring her thoughts as if they were live wires. What she hoped for was a clearer way to sit with her own heartbeat and to trust the people around her without constantly reading the room for danger. She sat on the edge of the chair, hands resting lightly on her knees, listening to the hum of the building, certain that whatever she faced next would be met with the same steady awareness that had carried her through the years.
